Chapter 1: The Weight of Tradition—How Caste Shapes Everyday Life.
Have you ever noticed how some of the most powerful divisions in society are the ones we almost never talk about?
In so many towns and villages, there’s this quiet rhythm—an unspoken order that shapes every part of daily life.
Who sits where, who shares a meal, even who’s allowed to touch what, or who’s expected to keep their distance... these aren’t just little habits.
For some, it all feels so normal—just the way things are. But for others, every rule is a reminder that they’re seen as less than.
Picture a child growing up in a small community, watching as their parents are turned away from certain homes, or seeing neighbors refuse to share water from the same well.
That child notices the subtle things—how some folks are always expected to serve, to clean, to stay out of sight. There’s a sting of shame in those moments... and confusion too.
Why should anyone be treated this way?
The answer, whispered by elders and reinforced by rituals, always comes down to the same thing: “It’s tradition. It’s our way.”
But let’s take a closer look at what tradition really means here.
This isn’t just about old habits or harmless customs—it’s a system that puts people into rigid boxes, deciding someone’s worth and dignity just because of where they were born.
The caste system, so deeply woven into the fabric of Hindu society, isn’t just a social arrangement.
It’s a hierarchy that touches every corner of a person’s life—what jobs they can have, who they can marry, even how they’re treated day to day.
For those at the bottom, especially the ones called “untouchable,” it’s a daily struggle with humiliation.
Most of the time, people don’t even realize how these lines shape every interaction.
Imagine a shopkeeper who won’t take money directly from certain customers, asking them to leave coins on the counter. Or a teacher who ignores a student’s questions, believing some minds just aren’t worth the effort.
Even when the whole community comes together for weddings, festivals, or meals, the lines are drawn—everyone knows exactly where they stand.
And this exclusion isn’t just about where you can go or what you can touch—it’s emotional too.
There’s this deep longing to belong, to be seen as equal, to join in fully with everyone else.
But the rules of caste are enforced not just by law or force, but by something even heavier: belief.
The idea that “this is how it’s always been, and how it must stay.”
Yet, under the surface, something else is growing.
Some folks start to question—why do these rules even exist?
They notice that the stories used to justify caste—those ancient texts, the warnings about purity—don’t really stand up to reason.
They see that the system mostly benefits a few, while so many pay the price.
And they realize: it’s not reason holding things together, it’s fear—and habit.
In these small moments of doubt, change begins to take root.
The first step is simple, but powerful—seeing that the caste system isn’t some natural law.
It’s something people invented. And if we made it, we can unmake it too.
